headline: Share your DSPi on the network, and Console now updates itself
items: DSPi Link shares the devices plugged into this Mac with phones, browsers and other Consoles on your local network. Switch it on under Settings > Networking, then pair each new client with a six-digit code and choose whether it can only watch, change settings, or administer the hub.
A browser on the same network can open the hub's address to reach a web control page served by Console itself.
Console can find devices shared by other Consoles on the network and lists them in the device menu, marked with the hub they live on.
Console can run quietly in the menu bar as a sharing gateway, and can start at login. Turn this on under Settings > Networking, or use Window > Minimise to Menu Bar (Cmd+Option+M).
Console checks for new releases and can download, verify and install them in place. Find it under Settings > Software Update, or choose Check for Updates from the app menu.
With firmware beta 5, slave mode tracks an S/PDIF, ADAT or I2S source far more closely and with cleaner output clocks, and the RP2350 accepts 4-channel 24-bit USB audio.
Changing the computer's volume is once again followed by the device.
Stats shows S/PDIF and I2S output buffer fill in fine steps, and its time since the last starvation keeps counting while the window is open.
I2S input data pins may use GPIOs parked on unused pairs, which are listed under Unused pairs.
Applying an AutoEQ profile trims only the two inputs it equalises, instead of every input on the device.
The main window's content now fills a tall window, and scrolled settings pages no longer draw over the title bar.

headline: Tube modelling, output limiters and filters you shape on the graph
items: The Tube Modeller gives each output the character of one of 16 popular vacuum tubes, with drive, mix and an output stage that recreates how a valve amplifier's transformer meets a loudspeaker. Find it under Tools > Tube Modeller (Cmd+Shift+D).

Every output now has its own brickwall limiter with adjustable threshold and release. Click the icon under an output's mute button to switch it on, or right-click it for settings. Linked outputs share their limiter settings, and the limiter also guards against test signals overdriving a tweeter.
Filters can now be edited directly on the response graph. Drag a band's dot to change its frequency and gain, scroll to change its width, and use the card beside it to pick a shape.
The effect windows are laid out in two columns, so their controls and graphs fit side by side.
The Matrix Mixer labels its input rows with the channel names.
Changing the computer's volume while listening to a non-USB input no longer shows a volume the device is not actually playing at.
DSPi Console uses much less CPU while connected to the device.

headline: A spectrum analyser, firmware updates and a guided start
items: A spectrum analyser shows the sound on any input or output as it plays. It appears above the filter list, on the dashboard for every output, and in its own window under Tools > Spectrum Analyser (Cmd+Shift+A). The device does the measuring, so it works with every source, including S/PDIF, ADAT and I2S.
The Subharmonic Synthesizer adds a new octave below the bass, for recordings that are light on low end. Find it under Tools > Subharmonic Synthesizer (Cmd+Shift+S).
Console now carries the matching firmware and installs it for you. If a connected device runs a different version, a banner offers a one-click update.
A setup wizard on first launch walks you through installing DSPi on a Pico. You can skip it, and run it again from the Help menu.
A short, optional tour of the main window is offered once, and advanced features explain themselves the first time you open them.
Control Surfaces can now switch auxiliary outputs: a relay, lamp or amplifier trigger on a spare GPIO pin.
Filter cards on the dashboard sit in a grid. Choose Auto or one to three per row from the gear on any card.
When a preset is loaded from the device itself, such as from a button or remote, the app now follows along.
